h1: Voltage Drop Calculator for Any Cable, AC or DC
author: ali-ahmad

fields.name: watts
fields.label: Load
fields.hint: Total watts the cable carries. Ignored if you enter the current below.

fields.name: amps
fields.label: Or current
fields.hint: If you know the current (from a label or clamp meter), enter it here and the watts are ignored. For three-phase, the current in one line.

fields.name: length_m
fields.label: Cable run, one way
fields.hint: Distance from the board or battery to the load along the cable route. The return conductor is counted for you.

fields.name: area_mm2
fields.label: Cable size
fields.hint: Conductor cross-section. Pakistani n/d cables are not exact metric sizes; enter the real conductor area: {{data.cables.pk_sizes.0.name}} is {{data.cables.pk_sizes.0.area_mm2|2}} mm², {{data.cables.pk_sizes.1.name}} is {{data.cables.pk_sizes.1.area_mm2|2}}, {{data.cables.pk_sizes.2.name}} is {{data.cables.pk_sizes.2.area_mm2|2}}, {{data.cables.pk_sizes.3.name}} is {{data.cables.pk_sizes.3.area_mm2|2}}, {{data.cables.pk_sizes.4.name}} is {{data.cables.pk_sizes.4.area_mm2|2}}. The current rating is checked at the next smaller standard size.

fields.name: conductor
fields.label: Conductor
fields.hint: Aluminium conducts less well, so the same size drops more voltage.

fields.name: mode
fields.label: Supply
fields.hint: Single-phase and DC count the cable twice (out and back); three-phase uses √3.

fields.name: volts
fields.label: Voltage
fields.hint: Leave blank for 230 V single-phase or 400 V three-phase line to line. For DC, enter the battery or string voltage.

fields.name: circuit
fields.label: Drop limit
fields.hint: The share of the supply voltage the cable may lose.

fields.name: pf
fields.label: Power factor
fields.hint: Used only to turn watts into amps on AC. 1 for heaters, about 0.8 for motors and mixed loads.

fields.name: rho
fields.label: Conductor resistivity
fields.hint: Leave blank to use the conductor chosen above: copper {{d.rho_copper|4}} or aluminium {{d.rho_aluminium|4}} Ω·mm²/m at working temperature. Enter a datasheet value to override it.

fields.name: ambient_c
fields.label: Air temperature around the cable
fields.hint: Hottest air the cable sits in: a conduit under a sunny roof or in a hot wall gets far hotter than the room. The default is a Pakistani summer value; every cable rating is reduced for it.

fields.name: circuits
fields.label: Circuits in the same conduit
fields.hint: How many circuits share this conduit or bundle. Cables packed together heat each other, so each one carries less.

answer: A {{out.amps|1}} A load on {{in.area_mm2|1}} mm² {{out.conductor}} cable over {{in.length_m|int}} m at {{in.volts|int}} V loses {{out.drop_v|1}} V, a voltage drop of {{out.drop_pct|2}}%, under the {{out.limit_pct|int}}% limit. Voltage drop = two × length × current × resistivity ÷ cable area for single-phase and DC; three-phase uses √3 instead of two. The cable must also be rated for the current, which the calculator checks for copper.
how: Current: {{out.amps|1}} A (the watts ÷ ({{out.k|4}} × {{out.volts|int}} V × {{out.pf|2}} power factor), unless you entered the amps). Drop = {{out.kv|4}} × {{in.length_m|int}} m × {{out.amps|1}} A × {{out.rho|4}} Ω·mm²/m ÷ {{in.area_mm2|2}} mm² = {{out.drop_v|1}} V, which is {{out.drop_pct|2}}% of {{out.volts|int}} V, leaving {{out.voltage_at_load|int}} V at the load. The current factor is one for single-phase and DC and √3 for three-phase; the drop factor is two (out and back) for single-phase and DC and √3 for three-phase. The limit you chose is {{out.limit_pct|int}}%; if the drop is over it, try the next cable size. A small drop does not make a cable safe: it must also be rated for the current.
key_facts: Voltage drop = 2 × length × current × resistivity ÷ area (single-phase and DC) or √3 × length × current × resistivity ÷ area (three-phase), with copper resistivity of {{d.rho_copper|4}} Ω·mm²/m at working temperature.
A {{out.amps|1}} A single-phase load on {{in.area_mm2|1}} mm² copper over {{in.length_m|int}} m drops {{out.drop_pct|2}}%; on {{ex.0.in.area_mm2|int}} mm² the drop falls to {{ex.0.out.drop_pct|2}}%.
The usual limits are {{d.vdrop_limit_lighting_pct|int}}% for lighting and solar DC and {{d.vdrop_limit_other_pct|int}}% for other circuits, measured from the supply to the load.

Low-voltage DC suffers most: {{ex.2.in.amps|int}} A from a {{ex.2.in.volts|int}} V battery over only {{ex.2.in.length_m|int}} m of {{ex.2.in.area_mm2|int}} mm² cable loses {{ex.2.out.drop_pct|1}}% of the voltage.

formula.text: ΔV = 2 × L × I × ρ ÷ A (single-phase, DC);  ΔV = √3 × L × I × ρ ÷ A (three-phase);  drop % = ΔV ÷ V × 100
lines: ΔV = volts lost in the cable
L = one-way cable length in metres
I = current in amps (from watts ÷ (V × PF), or watts ÷ (√3 × V × PF) on three-phase, if not entered; per line for three-phase)
ρ = conductor resistivity in Ω·mm²/m at working temperature (copper or aluminium)
A = conductor cross-section in mm²; V = supply voltage (line-to-line for three-phase)

p: The cable's resistance turns part of the voltage into heat. For single-phase and DC the current goes out on one conductor and back on the other, so the length counts twice: drop = 2 × length × current × resistivity ÷ area. For a balanced three-phase load the factor is √3 instead of two, and the drop is compared with the line-to-line voltage.

Halve the cable area and the drop doubles; double the length or the current and it doubles too. That is why long runs to a tubewell, gate or outbuilding need a thicker cable than the current alone suggests.

This calculator uses {{d.vdrop_limit_lighting_pct|int}}% for lighting circuits and {{d.vdrop_limit_other_pct|int}}% for other circuits, the values given in an informative annex of IEC 60364-5-52 for installations supplied from the public low-voltage network. Solar DC strings are usually kept to {{d.vdrop_limit_lighting_pct|int}}% so the panels lose little output. Above the limit, motors run hot, lights dim and inverters may trip on low voltage.

The drop limit is not the only test. A thin cable on a short run can show a tiny drop while carrying far more current than it is rated for, and overheat. For copper the calculator also compares the current with the cable's rating in conduit, corrected for the air temperature and the circuits sharing the conduit (Advanced settings), and warns when it is exceeded.

sections.h2: Cable voltage drop calculation, step by step
p: First the current: the load in watts ÷ ({{out.volts|int}} V × {{out.pf|2}} power factor) gives {{out.amps|1}} A for the default load. Then the drop: two × {{in.length_m|int}} m × {{out.amps|1}} A × copper resistivity ÷ {{in.area_mm2|1}} mm² = {{out.drop_v|1}} V. Finally the share: {{out.drop_v|1}} V of {{out.volts|int}} V is {{out.drop_pct|2}}%, under the {{out.limit_pct|int}}% limit, so {{out.voltage_at_load|int}} V reaches the load.

The drop grows in straight proportion to length, so the volts lost per metre stay fixed for a given cable and current. In the table below, the rows with the same cable size at different lengths show this: the longer run loses proportionally more. Divide the volts lost by the run to get your per-metre figure.

Choose DC and enter the battery or panel string voltage. At {{ex.2.in.volts|int}} V even a short cable loses a large share: {{ex.2.in.amps|int}} A over {{ex.2.in.length_m|int}} m of {{ex.2.in.area_mm2|int}} mm² loses {{ex.2.out.drop_v|2}} V, {{ex.2.out.drop_pct|1}}% of the supply. Keep battery cables short and thick, or move to a higher battery voltage. For solar panel strings, the solar DC cable calculator has the PV cable sizes.

Choose the conductor above. The calculator uses a resistivity of {{d.rho_copper|4}} Ω·mm²/m for copper and {{d.rho_aluminium|4}} Ω·mm²/m for aluminium, both at working temperature. Aluminium conducts less well than copper, so an aluminium cable of the same size drops more voltage: {{ex.4.in.area_mm2|int}} mm² aluminium over {{ex.4.in.length_m|int}} m drops {{ex.4.out.drop_pct|2}}% where copper drops {{ex.0.out.drop_pct|2}}%. That is why aluminium service and feeder cables are usually a size or two larger. The current rating is checked here for copper only; for aluminium, take it from the cable maker's datasheet. Copper and aluminium must never be joined directly; use bimetallic lugs or connectors.

mistakes: Entering the total out-and-back length. Enter the one-way run; the calculator already counts the return conductor.

Checking only one of the two. A cable can carry the current safely and still drop too much voltage over a long run, and a thin cable on a short run can pass the drop test while overheating; check both, as the wire size calculator does.
Leaving the conductor on copper for an aluminium cable. Aluminium drops more; choose Aluminium above.
Ignoring the drop on low-voltage DC. A drop that is trivial at {{d.v_1ph|int}} V can be several percent at {{ex.2.in.volts|int}} V over the same cable.
safety: Voltage drop is one check among several: the cable must also carry the current, match the breaker and suit how it is installed. Use the wire size calculator for the full check and have a licensed electrician select, install and test the cable.

faq.q: What is the voltage drop formula?
faq.a: Single-phase and DC: drop = 2 × length × current × resistivity ÷ cable area. Three-phase: drop = √3 × length × current × resistivity ÷ area. Copper resistivity is {{d.rho_copper|4}} Ω·mm²/m at working temperature.

faq.q: What is the maximum voltage drop allowed?
faq.a: This calculator checks {{d.vdrop_limit_lighting_pct|int}}% for lighting and {{d.vdrop_limit_other_pct|int}}% for other circuits, from the supply to the load. Solar DC strings are usually kept to {{d.vdrop_limit_lighting_pct|int}}%.

faq.q: How do I calculate voltage drop per metre?
faq.a: Work out the drop for your run and divide by its length; for the same cable and current the per-metre figure is fixed. Thicker cable or lower current reduces it.

faq.q: How much voltage drops on {{in.area_mm2|1}} mm² cable over {{in.length_m|int}} m?
faq.a: With {{out.amps|1}} A at {{in.volts|int}} V, {{out.drop_v|1}} V or {{out.drop_pct|2}}%. On {{ex.0.in.area_mm2|int}} mm² it is {{ex.0.out.drop_pct|2}}%.

faq.q: Does this voltage drop calculator work for DC?
faq.a: Yes. Choose DC and enter the battery or string voltage. {{ex.2.in.amps|int}} A at {{ex.2.in.volts|int}} V over {{ex.2.in.length_m|int}} m of {{ex.2.in.area_mm2|int}} mm² drops {{ex.2.out.drop_pct|1}}%.

faq.q: Can I calculate voltage drop for aluminium cable?
faq.a: Yes. Choose Aluminium as the conductor; the calculator then uses {{d.rho_aluminium|4}} Ω·mm²/m at working temperature instead of copper's {{d.rho_copper|4}}. {{ex.4.in.area_mm2|int}} mm² aluminium over {{ex.4.in.length_m|int}} m drops {{ex.4.out.drop_pct|2}}% with the default load. Check the aluminium cable's current rating in the maker's datasheet.

faq.q: What happens if the voltage drop is too high?
faq.a: Motors and compressors run hot and may fail to start, lights dim, and inverters or stabilisers may cut out. Use a larger cable, shorten the run, or split the load.
